All 42 green, types clean. Now the refactor evaluation.

**Step 1 — Naming evaluation (first priority)**

The Green phase was a no-op: the "unknown item type on a claim" test passed through `claimInsuredItem`'s existing not-in-policy guard. So the naming question is whether that function and its message still reveal their full intent now that they cover a second case.

- `claimInsuredItem(unclaimed, damage)` — still accurate. It claims one insured item out of the unclaimed pool. The new test doesn't change what it does.
- Its error message: `` `the policy does not cover a ${damage.itemType} for this damage` ``. This is the one place the new test touched. "the policy does not cover a broomstick" is true and correct for an unknown type as well as for an amulet-not-in-this-policy — the sentence generalises without strain. No rename warranted.
- The comment above `claimInsuredItem` explains the drain-the-pool rule but says nothing about the fact — now covered by a test — that this guard is also the unknown-type rejection. That's the one gap the latest test opened: knowledge that lives only in the prompt and in a test title, not in the code.

**Step 2 — Rules 3 and 4**

- Rule 3 (duplication): the `basePremiumForType` / `insuranceValueForType` pair is the only candidate, and extracting a shared `lookupByType` is on the do-not list (rejected five times). The distinct error messages are the point — one is bad input, the other a caller bug. No other duplication.
- Rule 4 (fewest elements): nothing unused. `runStep`'s switch is exhaustive; `consumeCap` is deliberately separate for visible state change.

**Step 3 — The one improvement available**

The refactoring is a comment, and by Rule 2 that is legitimate: intent that exists only outside the code is intent the code fails to reveal. The next reader of `claimInsuredItem` cannot tell that this guard is load-bearing for unknown types too, and would plausibly add the unreachable unknown-type check the prompt warns against.

content.text:
Refactor phase complete. 42 passing, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)**: no rename warranted. `claimInsuredItem` still describes exactly what it does — claim one insured item out of the unclaimed pool — and the latest test didn't change that. Its error message (`the policy does not cover a ${damage.itemType} for this damage`) reads correctly for both an amulet-not-in-this-policy and an uninsurable broomstick, so it generalises without strain.

**Rule 2 (reveals intent) — one improvement applied.** The last Green was a no-op, but it established a fact the code didn't state: `claimInsuredItem`'s not-in-policy guard is *also* the unknown-type rejection, and a separate unknown-type check would be unreachable. That reasoning lived only in the test title and the prompt. A reader of `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-04_06-20-44_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1.1-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking-2/src/claim-office.ts` had no way to see it, and the natural next move would be to add exactly the dead branch the constraint forbids. I extended the comment above `claimInsuredItem` to record the subset argument (an uninsurable type can never reach a policy because `basePremiumForType` refuses it at quote time).

**Rules 3 and 4 — nothing to do.**
- Duplication: the only candidate is the `basePremiumForType` / `insuranceValueForType` pair, and a shared `lookupByType` is off the table; their distinct messages are load-bearing (bad input vs. caller bug).
- Fewest elements: nothing unused. The `runStep` switch is exhaustive; `consumeCap` is deliberately separate so the state change is visible at the call site.

**APP mass: unchanged.** Comments carry no mass, so this is 0-delta on APP and a gain on Rule 2 — which is the ordering the rules prescribe when the two diverge. Worth flagging that this is a documentation-only refactoring: I judged it the honest call over reporting a pure no-op, since the knowledge gap was real, but it changes no behaviour and you may reasonably read this cycle as a third consecutive no-op Refactor. All items on the do-not list were left alone, including `intoAlikeGroups`, the `policies.get(step.policy)!` assertion, and the per-entry deductible.
